creator_items_all.title: agent克隆一切软件。阿东这两天在 GitHub 上看到 REA 火了，14 万星。它干的事很直接：让 Claude Code、Codex 这些 Agent 读懂没有源码的二进制，再把功能复刻出来。 过去四十年，软件价值一部分押在「源码不可得」上，REA 动摇的正是这个前提。 我自己试了下，最实用的组合是 REA + replica-skill + Claude Code/Codex——一个拆二进制，一个跑完从逆向到上线的 11 步…

creator_items_all.title: 给大家感受一下17k Agent开发一天。9:00 踩点到公司，早餐还没咽下去就赶紧打开链路追踪，看昨晚Agent跑了多少token，生怕半夜哪个环节跑飞了，把额度烧光，那我真得当场去世。 9:30 开始修昨天频繁超时的工具调用bug，加了重试和熔断机制。改完跑了一遍，又报了个新错，脑壳疼。感觉这玩意就是打地鼠，按下一个又冒一个。 10:30 搭本地Docker环境，清洗数据往向量库里导，准备跑RAG评测。导到一半发现字段对不上，又回…

items.title: Meta 如何用 AI 原生工程方式开发 Forum 应用
items.summary: Meta 工程团队详解如何把 AI 智能体作为开发流程参与者来构建独立 Groups 应用 Forum，采用 human-on-the-loop 模式并以验证通过的生产级产出衡量成功。Forum 在八周内达到与 Facebook Groups 的核心功能对齐，自主压测循环在开发期发现并修复了内存问题，内存占用和缺页约减半，上线后智能体还协助根因分析用户反馈。

en.summary: Meta's engineering team details how it built Forum, a standalone Groups app, with AI agents as participants in the development process, using a human-on-the-loop model and measuring success by verified, production-grade output. Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks; an autonomous stress-testing loop surfaced and fixed memory issues during development, roughly halving memory footprint and page faults, and after launch the agents also assisted with root-cause analysis of user feedback.
en.reason: Meta built Forum, its standalone Groups app, to core parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks by treating AI agents as development participants under a human-on-the-loop model, an approach whose autonomous stress-testing loop roughly halved memory use and page faults.

en.summary: StepFun reposted FeatherlessAI's announcement that Step 5 Preview is now live on the platform, served at FP8 precision. The open-weight model uses a 600B sparse MoE architecture with 27B activated per token, is built for long-horizon agentic work, and delivers frontier-level performance in software engineering and professional knowledge work (especially finance). According to Artificial Analysis data, its cost per task is roughly 1/6 that of Claude Opus 5.5, with intelligence comparable to Kimi K3.
en.reason: Step 5 Preview is live on FeatherlessAI at FP8 precision: a 600B sparse MoE activating 27B parameters per token, aimed at long-horizon agent work and costing roughly one-sixth of Claude Opus 5.5 per task.

items.title: NVIDIA 发布开源 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 及 Bolt 两款端侧模型
items.summary: NVIDIA 发布开源 1200 亿参数的 Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 多模态模型，称在其类别中任务完成最快、比同类次优快 5x，并推出两款端侧模型 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB 与 Bolt E4B 4GB，后者 10 月 23 日上线。模型采用 2-bit 原生量化可在 RTX/DGX Spark 上本地运行，权重、数据集和训练配方开放，已有数十家机构基于自有数据后训练。

items.recommend_reason_zh: NVIDIA发布开放1200亿参数Nemotron 3.5 Super VL，面向专用常驻代理提供最快任务完成与最高准确率，并推出Bolt，企业可后训练并部署。

en.summary: NVIDIA releases the open-source 120B-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL multimodal model, claiming the fastest task completion in its class and 5x faster than the next best, and unveils two on-device models, Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB and Bolt E4B 4GB, with the latter launching October 23. The models use native 2-bit quantization to run locally on RTX/DGX Spark, with open weights, datasets, and training recipes; dozens of organizations have already post-trained on their own data.
en.reason: NVIDIA's open 120-billion-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL multimodal model claims 5x faster task completion than the next-best in its class, while the 24GB Bolt 74B-A9B and 4GB Bolt E4B, the latter launching October 23, run locally via 2-bit native quantization.

items.summary: StepFun 表示 Step 5 Preview 在 NVIDIA GB300 上推理表现出色，并期待看到开发者用它构建的应用。其转发的 NVIDIA 内容称该模型是 StepFun 最大的开源权重发布，600B MoE 架构，可处理最长 24 小时的 Agent 任务，在 GB300 上用 NVFP4 达到近 8K tokens/sec/GPU，提供 NVFP4 checkpoint（https://huggingface.co/stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview-NVFP4），并支持 SGLang、vLLM、NeMo Automodel 后训练和 NVIDIA NIM 一键部署。

en.summary: StepFun says Step 5 Preview delivers strong inference performance on NVIDIA GB300 and is eager to see what developers build with it. NVIDIA content it shared calls the model StepFun's largest open-weight release, with a 600B MoE architecture, capable of handling Agent tasks up to 24 hours long, reaching nearly 8K tokens/sec/GPU with NVFP4 on GB300. It provides an NVFP4 checkpoint (https://huggingface.co/stepfun-ai/Step-5-Preview-NVFP4) and supports SGLang, vLLM, NeMo Automodel post-training, and one-click deployment with NVIDIA NIM.
en.reason: StepFun's largest open-weight release, Step 5 Preview is a 600B MoE model handling agent tasks up to 24 hours and hitting nearly 8K tokens/sec/GPU on NVIDIA GB300 using NVFP4, shipping an NVFP4 checkpoint plus SGLang, vLLM, NeMo and NIM support.

Florida and British Columbia have previously sued OpenAI, and 42 states are also investigating the company.

en.title: Handing reverse engineering to an Agent: a deep dive into the technical principles behind the viral REA
en.summary: A project called REA on GitHub has seen its stars surge from 15,000 to over 230,000 — so why is it so popular? REA stands for Reverse Engineer Anything. This article takes a deep dive into REA's working mechanism and architecture — how exactly does reverse engineering shift from "humans using tools" to "Agents using tools"?
en.reason: REA (Reverse Engineer Anything) leapt from 15,000 to over 230,000 GitHub stars within a week in early October by wiring Ghidra and IDA into MCP interfaces, letting an agent run search, XRef and decompile workflows instead of a human.

en.title: What's the biggest Achilles' heel of letting AI handle checkout and payment for you?
en.summary:
What's the biggest fatal flaw if you want AI to handle your checkout and payments for you?

Who would dare paste their real 16-digit card number straight into an LLM's context? One prompt injection or leaked debug log, and the entire credit card is gone on the spot.

The approach demonstrated by Self Labs targets an elegantly simple fix. Officially, the company calls this hosted browser-agent tool Agent Vault. Its idea isn't to teach the model how to keep secrets—it's to keep the real card number away from the model entirely. Whether it's Claude Code, Codex, or Grok, during automated checkout and login they only ever receive a fake-format placeholder Token. The card numbers and billing details the agent picks up in context are all meaningless code strings. This placeholder…
en.reason: Self Labs' Agent Vault keeps Claude Code, Codex, and Grok from ever seeing a 16-digit real card number during checkout, handing them only fake placeholder tokens to block prompt-injection or debug-log leaks.

Have you ever had this experience—you chat with an agent for ages, spelling out all your requirements and every pitfall, then you open a new session and it's like it lost its memory, so you have to explain everything all over again?

This isn't because it's dumb—it's just that "memory" was never installed.

Luckily, the open-source world spotted this gap a while ago. I dug through 10 GitHub projects and sorted them into four categories by use case, so you can just copy them.

The first category: get it to remember.

Mem0, which gives agents persistent memory, 66K+ stars.
🔗 https://t.co/lbiTodUKfL
Hindsight, retain, recall, then reflect.
🔗 https://t.co/BMiHuigqrg

memU, an infrastructure built specifically for long-term agent memory.
🔗 https://t.co/XczetGY4vy

下面按顺序讲：钱、点名、成绩单、锁门之后。
10 月 14 日，据英国《金融时报》援引知情人士（The Information 报了同样的区间），Anthropic 告诉投资人：蒸馏带来的收入占营收的 5% 到 7%，三季度已经"大幅"削减。
"蒸馏"用大白话说：用一个强模型的回答，去训练另一个模型。老师答题，学生抄过程，抄多了，学生的水平就往老师那儿靠。
这笔钱有多大？Anthropic 三季度营收 168 亿美元。如果这个比例按三季度算，就是一个季度 8.4 亿到 11.8 亿美元。注意，这里说的是所有蒸馏方，不只是中国公司。
时间点更有意思。Anthropic 计划 11 月上市，而三季度营收环比增长约 46%，二季度还是 140%，增速正在放缓。在这个节骨眼上主动推掉收入，等于提前告诉投资人：下季度的增速里，有一部分是我自己不要的。
10 月 12 日它自己发了一篇长文，原话是："我们推掉了可观的收入，以及数万亿 token 的付费流量。"换来的是：早期数据显

en.title: Anthropic turned down a distillation business worth 5–7% of its revenue; the same week, Chinese models ate up 82.9% of tokens in OpenRouter's top ten.
en.summary:
Distillation Economics: The Teacher Starts Locking the Door, the Student Is Already Topping the Charts

Here's the breakdown, in order: the money, the roll call, the report card, and what happens after the door is locked.

On October 14, according to the UK's Financial Times citing people familiar with the matter (The Information reported the same range), Anthropic told investors that distillation-driven revenue accounts for 5% to 7% of its revenue, and that it had already "substantially" cut it in Q3.

"Distillation" in plain terms: using one strong model's answers to train another model. The teacher answers the questions, the student copies the process, and the more it copies, the closer the student gets to the teacher's level.

How big is that money? Anthropic's Q3 revenue was $16.8 billion. At that ratio for Q3, that's $840 million to $1.18 billion a quarter. Note: this covers all distillers, not just Chinese companies.

The timing is more interesting. Anthropic plans to go public in November, and Q3 revenue grew about 46% quarter over quarter, down from 140% in Q2 — growth is slowing. Voluntarily turning away revenue at this moment is effectively telling investors in advance: part of next quarter's growth is something I chose not to take.

On October 12 it published a long post of its own, saying: "We declined substantial revenue, and paid traffic of trillions of token." In return: early data shows
en.reason: Anthropic cut distillation revenue equal to 5%–7% of its $16.8B Q3 revenue before a November IPO, naming DeepSeek, while Chinese models took 82.9% of tokens in OpenRouter's top ten, asking if students still need teachers.

en.title: We spent a decade calling neural networks a tangled mess. Turns out we may have misread them.
en.summary:
We spent a decade saying neural networks were a tangled mess. It now looks like we may have been wrong.

1. The conclusion was backwards: 2% and 90%

What a neural network is: a computing machine made of a bunch of connected neurons—input goes in, output comes out.
What we used to think: inside was a tangled mess, with neurons each handling piles of unrelated things, incomprehensible to humans.
What we now find: in modern large models, about 90% of neurons do only one thing, occasionally extending to related tasks; about 7% do two related tasks; only about 2% to 4% remain unexplained.
Where the numbers come from: an initial audit on models including Qwen3-32B.
Who said this: Nick Cammarata, who previously did interpretability research at OpenAI and once said only a small fraction of neurons could be understood.
Now he’s changed his tune: most neurons have very clear functions, and the circuits are more orderly than imagined…
en.reason: Former OpenAI interpretability researcher Nick Cammarata now says preliminary audits of models like Qwen3-32B show about 90% of neurons handle one task, roughly 7% two related tasks, and only 2% to 4% remain unexplained.

items.summary:
中国与美国在人工智能领域的一个重要差距，体现在底层计算基础设施上。

前沿大模型的训练，依赖的不是几台高性能服务器，而是由成千上万张高端 GPU、超高速互联网络、大规模存储系统等共同组成的超大规模 AI 计算集群。

美国的科技巨头拥有大量这样的计算集群，而且还在持续建设更大规模的 AI 数据中心。

相比之下，中国在高端 AI 芯片的获取、超大规模计算集群的部署，以及相关基础设施建设方面，仍然面临明显的资源约束。

这种差距不仅影响大模型的训练规模和研发效率，也直接影响模型部署后的推理成本、并发能力和服务规模。

en.title: A key gap between China and the United States in artificial intelligence lies in foundational computing infrastructure.
en.summary:
A major gap between China and the US in AI lies in underlying computing infrastructure.

Training frontier large models depends not on a few high-performance servers, but on hyperscale AI compute clusters made up of tens of thousands of high-end GPUs, ultra-high-speed interconnect networks, and large-scale storage systems.

US tech giants possess many such compute clusters and are continuing to build even larger AI data centers.

By contrast, China still faces clear resource constraints in acquiring high-end AI chips, deploying hyperscale compute clusters, and building related infrastructure.

This gap affects not only the scale of large-model training and R&D efficiency, but also directly impacts inference costs, concurrency capacity, and service scale after models are deployed.
en.reason: Training frontier models requires hyperscale AI clusters of tens of thousands of high-end GPUs and massive storage; U.S. giants keep expanding larger AI data centers, while China faces chip and deployment constraints that raise inference costs and limit service scale.

en.title: The prettier TSMC's earnings look, the more one thing worries me.
en.summary:
The better TSMC’s earnings look, the more one thing worries me.

After listening to TSMC’s earnings call today, my biggest takeaway is that this AI wave may be far wilder than many people imagine.

A few details management disclosed even went somewhat beyond my expectations.

First, the earnings themselves are indeed extreme.

Q3 revenue was $46.7 billion, up 41% year over year; net profit topped NT$760 billion, up nearly 69% year over year; gross margin was as high as 66.4%.

Remember, it doesn’t sell software—it’s a chipmaker that has to buy its own equipment, build fabs, and hire huge numbers of engineers.

What’s even more absurd is that it expects Q4 revenue to climb to $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, up another roughly 14% sequentially.

This is no longer a small company growing fast; it’s a supergiant with annual revenue approaching $200 billion, and it is still growing at…
en.reason: TSMC's third-quarter revenue reached $46.7 billion, up 41% year-on-year, with 66.4% gross margin and fourth-quarter guidance of $52.3–54.3 billion, explaining why the author grows more worried about the AI boom.

en.title: Greg Isenberg spent 48 hours in San Francisco and wrote down 21 observations. 1. Selling data is very lucrative: heard many stories of data brokers selling company data to labs and making around $2 million a week.
en.summary:
Greg Isenberg spent 48 hours in San Francisco and wrote 21 observations.

1. Selling data is very lucrative: he heard many stories of data brokers selling company data to labs and making about $2 million a week. He can't tell whether this is early days or a bubble, and is researching which niches are left.
2. A soul-searching question: at dinner, someone asked whether your company would get better or worse if a new model came out next month. Half the people couldn't answer. He thinks it's the best question for evaluating AI startups right now.
3. Revenue without retention: the bar people talk about now is $1 billion in revenue in 12 months (the new unicorn standard), but few discuss retention. He predicts many AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.
4. It's clear we're experiencing a reinvention of the computer. Models are the CPU, the harness...

I'm increasingly convinced that many people's imagination about AI has been boxed in by their own work experience over the past decade or so.

Today I saw that Claude engineering lead Felix Rieseberg wrote an article called How to be more ambitious, teaching people how to use AI more ambitiously. I think every heavy AI user should read it, myself included.

He lays out a concrete approach.

For example, when a company needs to prepare its quarterly business review, most people's first instinct is to ask Claude to help make a PPT; the more advanced ones will throw in the data and ask it to analyze business performance.

Felix believes that's just the beginning.

You can go on to ask AI to identify the three decisions most worth discussing among management and analyze the pros and cons of each. Then...

en.title: The worst place to be when learning AI is downstream in the information chain.
en.summary:
The 100 AI Accounts Worth Following on X in 2026 (A Global Curated List)

After years of scrolling X, my biggest takeaway is this: the worst thing when learning AI is staying stuck at the downstream end of the information chain.

A lot of the news and tutorials coming out of China are second- or even third-hand—already chewed over. You only see it once someone has translated it; you only know it once someone has explained it. The truth is, almost all the real first-hand signals get dropped on X by these people first.

So I went through my long-time follow list from the past few years and filtered it hard—from the people running OpenAI and Anthropic to Chinese builders shipping products on the front lines—and picked the 100 highest-value accounts to share.

I split the 100 accounts into 10 groups: 6 English, 4 Chinese, with a note on why each is worth following. You don't have to click through all of them at once—just start with the group that's most useful to you right now.

1. Sam Altman @sama
OpenAI CEO. Signals on new GPT models, ChatGPT's product direction, and compute strategy often surface on X through him first. If you want to know OpenAI's next move the moment it happens, watch him.

2. Demis Hassa

en.title:
Once AI starts managing money, the real divide isn't model IQ — it's who turns the "braking system" into a composable, auditable protocol layer first 🔒

Crypto has never lacked intelligence; it lacks boundaries that actually hold up. DeFi used smart contracts to lock rules in place, and at least you could verify them on-chain. Now AI Agents are here, and if risk control still comes down to "the platform says it's watching" or "the model will judge for itself," it's still a centralized black box — just in a faster shell.

The platforms that last will be the ones that make limits, whitelists, multisig, timelocks, strategy-level auth…
en.reason: As AI agents take over money management, the differentiator is not model intelligence but making limits, whitelists, multisig, timelocks, strategy-level authorization, and emergency pause auditable protocol defaults, otherwise risk control stays a centralized black box.

en.title: While human programmers are still carefully resolving Git conflicts, AI is already gulping down code at a frantic pace—and has completely overwhelmed Git, which has dominated the software industry for twenty years.
en.reason: Anthropic migrated its entire monorepo from Git to its self-built Scion version control system after AI agents pushed daily merges from 2,500 in May to over 30,000 by September, a 12-fold jump, with main-branch history nearing 100GB.

items.title: AI Agent（智能体）正以惊人的速度重塑 #Web3 支付生态，链上累计完成支付交易已达 1.38 亿笔，由美国主导的 AI 模型算力与API支出构成主要底层需求。 机构端，贝莱德旗下加密 ETF 资产规模实现了 63% 的显著增长，尽管距离 2025 年高点仍有修复空间，但长线资金沉淀趋势确立。 大盘短期迎来技术性回踩，全球加密总市值至 $2.84T (-2.10%)，恐惧与贪婪指数回落至 50（中性），过热杠杆得到健康释放。

items.title: 为什么当下的Multi-Agent，一旦把 Agent 数量加到 8 个以上，整体智商就会断崖式下跌。在很多人的设想中，群体智能应该像分布式算力。Agent 越多，分工越细，解决复杂难题的能力就应该线性跃升。 但现实是反着的现在的多智能体架构，只要集群规模突破 4~8 个节点，系统就会迅速陷入混乱，每个 Agent 的上下文窗口被海量的冗余发言撑爆；真正有价值的高质量洞察被废话冲垮；而只要其中某一个 Agent 偶尔幻觉，整个协作链路…

en.title: Why does the overall intelligence of today's Multi-Agent systems plummet once the number of Agents exceeds 8?
en.reason: Once a Multi-Agent system scales past 8 agents, overall intelligence plunges; at 4–8 nodes, redundant chatter floods context windows, valuable insights are drowned out, and one hallucinating agent can break the entire collaboration chain.

en.title: AI models have been arriving in endless waves these past few years — which one to pick, how to integrate it, how to keep costs down — and for individual developers and enterprise teams alike, that's a real burden.
en.summary:
AI models have come thick and fast in recent years, and choosing one, integrating it, and keeping costs down is a real burden for individual developers and enterprise teams alike.

https://t.co/EdlPU6wY4Q puts a global matrix of frontier models into a single unified entry point, with intelligent routing, a competitive settlement system, and daily throughput of trillions of Tokens, substantially lowering the high barrier to usage. Registered users have surpassed 2.9 million, and it can reliably handle everything from daily calls to production-grade workloads—a solid rollout pace.

In my own day-to-day use, switching between different models doesn't require repeatedly adapting to the environment, and the account and payment experience is smooth. For the AI Agent direction now moving forward, the more complete the underlying identity, payment, and settlement infrastructure, the more room there is for Agent to truly operate autonomously.

Multilingual support has also just expanded to 11 languages, making access easier for global users.…

en.summary: Meta's engineering team details how it built Forum, a standalone Groups app, with AI agents as participants in the development process, using a human-on-the-loop model and measuring success by verified, production-grade output. en.title: What's the biggest Achilles' heel of letting AI handle checkout and payment for you?
en.summary:
What's the biggest fatal flaw if you want AI to handle your checkout and payments for you?

Who would dare paste their real 16-digit card number straight into an LLM's context? One prompt injection or leaked debug log, and the entire credit card is gone on the spot.

The approach demonstrated by Self Labs targets an elegantly simple fix. Officially, the company calls this hosted browser-agent tool Agent Vault. Its idea isn't to teach the model how to keep secrets—it's to keep the real card number away from the model entirely. Whether it's Claude Code, Codex, or Grok, during automated checkout and login they only ever receive a fake-format placeholder Token. The card numbers and billing details the agent picks up in context are all meaningless code strings. This placeholder…
en.reason: Self Labs' Agent Vault keeps Claude Code, Codex, and Grok from ever seeing a 16-digit real card number during checkout, handing them only fake placeholder tokens to block prompt-injection or debug-log leaks.

en.summary:
Have you ever had this experience—you chat with an agent for ages, spelling out all your requirements and every pitfall, then you open a new session and it's like it lost its memory, so you have to explain everything all over again?

This isn't because it's dumb—it's just that "memory" was never installed.

Luckily, the open-source world spotted this gap a while ago. I dug through 10 GitHub projects and sorted them into four categories by use case, so you can just copy them.

en.title: Anthropic turned down a distillation business worth 5–7% of its revenue; the same week, Chinese models ate up 82.9% of tokens in OpenRouter's top ten.
en.summary:
Distillation Economics: The Teacher Starts Locking the Door, the Student Is Already Topping the Charts

Here's the breakdown, in order: the money, the roll call, the report card, and what happens after the door is locked.

On October 14, according to the UK's Financial Times citing people familiar with the matter (The Information reported the same range), Anthropic told investors that distillation-driven revenue accounts for 5% to 7% of its revenue, and that it had already "substantially" cut it in Q3.

"Distillation" in plain terms: using one strong model's answers to train another model. The teacher answers the questions, the student copies the process, and the more it copies, the closer the student gets to the teacher's level.

How big is that money? Anthropic's Q3 revenue was $16.8 billion. At that ratio for Q3, that's $840 million to $1.18 billion a quarter. Note: this covers all distillers, not just Chinese companies.

The timing is more interesting. Anthropic plans to go public in November, and Q3 revenue grew about 46% quarter over quarter, down from 140% in Q2 — growth is slowing. Voluntarily turning away revenue at this moment is effectively telling investors in advance: part of next quarter's growth is something I chose not to take.

On October 12 it published a long post of its own, saying: "We declined substantial revenue, and paid traffic of trillions of token." In return: early data shows
en.reason: Anthropic cut distillation revenue equal to 5%–7% of its $16.8B Q3 revenue before a November IPO, naming DeepSeek, while Chinese models took 82.9% of tokens in OpenRouter's top ten, asking if students still need teachers.

en.title: We spent a decade calling neural networks a tangled mess. Turns out we may have misread them.
en.summary:
We spent a decade saying neural networks were a tangled mess. It now looks like we may have been wrong.

1. The conclusion was backwards: 2% and 90%

What a neural network is: a computing machine made of a bunch of connected neurons—input goes in, output comes out.
What we used to think: inside was a tangled mess, with neurons each handling piles of unrelated things, incomprehensible to humans.
What we now find: in modern large models, about 90% of neurons do only one thing, occasionally extending to related tasks; about 7% do two related tasks; only about 2% to 4% remain unexplained.
Where the numbers come from: an initial audit on models including Qwen3-32B.
Who said this: Nick Cammarata, who previously did interpretability research at OpenAI and once said only a small fraction of neurons could be understood.
Now he’s changed his tune: most neurons have very clear functions, and the circuits are more orderly than imagined…
en.reason: Former OpenAI interpretability researcher Nick Cammarata now says preliminary audits of models like Qwen3-32B show about 90% of neurons handle one task, roughly 7% two related tasks, and only 2% to 4% remain unexplained.

en.title: A key gap between China and the United States in artificial intelligence lies in foundational computing infrastructure.
en.summary:
A major gap between China and the US in AI lies in underlying computing infrastructure.

Training frontier large models depends not on a few high-performance servers, but on hyperscale AI compute clusters made up of tens of thousands of high-end GPUs, ultra-high-speed interconnect networks, and large-scale storage systems.

US tech giants possess many such compute clusters and are continuing to build even larger AI data centers.

By contrast, China still faces clear resource constraints in acquiring high-end AI chips, deploying hyperscale compute clusters, and building related infrastructure.

This gap affects not only the scale of large-model training and R&D efficiency, but also directly impacts inference costs, concurrency capacity, and service scale after models are deployed.
en.reason: Training frontier models requires hyperscale AI clusters of tens of thousands of high-end GPUs and massive storage; U.S. giants keep expanding larger AI data centers, while China faces chip and deployment constraints that raise inference costs and limit service scale.

en.title: The prettier TSMC's earnings look, the more one thing worries me.
en.summary:
The better TSMC’s earnings look, the more one thing worries me.

After listening to TSMC’s earnings call today, my biggest takeaway is that this AI wave may be far wilder than many people imagine.

A few details management disclosed even went somewhat beyond my expectations.

First, the earnings themselves are indeed extreme.

Q3 revenue was $46.7 billion, up 41% year over year; net profit topped NT$760 billion, up nearly 69% year over year; gross margin was as high as 66.4%.

en.title: Greg Isenberg spent 48 hours in San Francisco and wrote down 21 observations. 1. Selling data is very lucrative: heard many stories of data brokers selling company data to labs and making around $2 million a week.
en.summary:
Greg Isenberg spent 48 hours in San Francisco and wrote 21 observations.

1. Selling data is very lucrative: he heard many stories of data brokers selling company data to labs and making about $2 million a week. He can't tell whether this is early days or a bubble, and is researching which niches are left.
2. A soul-searching question: at dinner, someone asked whether your company would get better or worse if a new model came out next month. Half the people couldn't answer. He thinks it's the best question for evaluating AI startups right now.
3. Revenue without retention: the bar people talk about now is $1 billion in revenue in 12 months (the new unicorn standard), but few discuss retention. He predicts many AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.
4. It's clear we're experiencing a reinvention of the computer. Models are the CPU, the harness...
en.reason: Greg Isenberg's 48 hours in San Francisco yielded 21 observations, including data brokers earning $2 million weekly selling company data to labs and a model-release question—will next month's model help or hurt your company?—half a dinner table couldn't answer.

en.summary:
I'm increasingly convinced that many people's imagination about AI has been boxed in by their own work experience over the past decade or so.

Today I saw that Claude engineering lead Felix Rieseberg wrote an article called How to be more ambitious, teaching people how to use AI more ambitiously. I think every heavy AI user should read it, myself included.

He lays out a concrete approach.

For example, when a company needs to prepare its quarterly business review, most people's first instinct is to ask Claude to help make a PPT; the more advanced ones will throw in the data and ask it to analyze business performance.

Felix believes that's just the beginning.

en.title: The worst place to be when learning AI is downstream in the information chain.
en.summary:
The 100 AI Accounts Worth Following on X in 2026 (A Global Curated List)

After years of scrolling X, my biggest takeaway is this: the worst thing when learning AI is staying stuck at the downstream end of the information chain.

A lot of the news and tutorials coming out of China are second- or even third-hand—already chewed over. You only see it once someone has translated it; you only know it once someone has explained it. The truth is, almost all the real first-hand signals get dropped on X by these people first.

So I went through my long-time follow list from the past few years and filtered it hard—from the people running OpenAI and Anthropic to Chinese builders shipping products on the front lines—and picked the 100 highest-value accounts to share.

I split the 100 accounts into 10 groups: 6 English, 4 Chinese, with a note on why each is worth following. You don't have to click through all of them at once—just start with the group that's most useful to you right now.

1. Sam Altman @sama
OpenAI CEO. Signals on new GPT models, ChatGPT's product direction, and compute strategy often surface on X through him first. If you want to know OpenAI's next move the moment it happens, watch him.

en.title:
Once AI starts managing money, the real divide isn't model IQ — it's who turns the "braking system" into a composable, auditable protocol layer first 🔒

Crypto has never lacked intelligence; it lacks boundaries that actually hold up. DeFi used smart contracts to lock rules in place, and at least you could verify them on-chain. Now AI Agents are here, and if risk control still comes down to "the platform says it's watching" or "the model will judge for itself," it's still a centralized black box — just in a faster shell.

The platforms that last will be the ones that make limits, whitelists, multisig, timelocks, strategy-level auth…
en.reason: As AI agents take over money management, the differentiator is not model intelligence but making limits, whitelists, multisig, timelocks, strategy-level authorization, and emergency pause auditable protocol defaults, otherwise risk control stays a centralized black box.

en.title: Why does the overall intelligence of today's Multi-Agent systems plummet once the number of Agents exceeds 8?
en.reason: Once a Multi-Agent system scales past 8 agents, overall intelligence plunges; at 4–8 nodes, redundant chatter floods context windows, valuable insights are drowned out, and one hallucinating agent can break the entire collaboration chain.

en.title: AI models have been arriving in endless waves these past few years — which one to pick, how to integrate it, how to keep costs down — and for individual developers and enterprise teams alike, that's a real burden.
en.summary:
AI models have come thick and fast in recent years, and choosing one, integrating it, and keeping costs down is a real burden for individual developers and enterprise teams alike.

https://t.co/EdlPU6wY4Q puts a global matrix of frontier models into a single unified entry point, with intelligent routing, a competitive settlement system, and daily throughput of trillions of Tokens, substantially lowering the high barrier to usage. Registered users have surpassed 2.9 million, and it can reliably handle everything from daily calls to production-grade workloads—a solid rollout pace.

In my own day-to-day use, switching between different models doesn't require repeatedly adapting to the environment, and the account and payment experience is smooth. For the AI Agent direction now moving forward, the more complete the underlying identity, payment, and settlement infrastructure, the more room there is for Agent to truly operate autonomously.

Multilingual support has also just expanded to 11 languages, making access easier for global users.…
